intro: The guests arrive to a march; the middle of Grieg’s Wedding Day at Troldhaugen turns into a quiet duet. Harald Vetter plays the whole celebration, including its wonderfully blunt last chord.

sections.label: A · The D major march
sections.mNote: Low octaves, clipped chords and a quick triplet

sections.label: B · The march fills the keyboard
sections.mNote: Octaves and chords give the tune more weight

sections.label: C · A quiet duet in G major
sections.mNote: The melody passes between the pianist’s hands

sections.label: D · The D major march returns
sections.mNote: Tempo I brings back the opening march

sections.label: E · Fading triplets and one last chord
sections.mNote: The piano retreats to ppp, then strikes a final fff

cues.title: A march with a skip
cues.text: The left hand puts a low D beneath short chords. Then a quick triplet sends the melody on its way. Grieg’s marking is Tempo di Marcia un poco vivace: a march with a little life in it. The bass supplies the boots; the tune is already dancing.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Op. 65 No. 6, bars 1–10, Louis Oesterle edition, typeset by David Whipple for Mutopia: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/GriegE/O65/troldhaugen/troldhaugen-a4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The well-wishers are coming
cues.text: At Grieg’s silver wedding anniversary, more guests turn up at Troldhaugen than he and Nina have invited. He remembers the gathering in this piece, written in 1896. Its first title, “The well-wishers are coming”, puts the visitors on the path to the house.
cues.evidence: Ernst-Günter Heinemann and Einar Steen-Nøkleberg, preface to Henle HN 1291 (2016), pp. III–IV: silver wedding, unexpected guests, composition in summer 1896 and autograph title “Die Gratulanten kommen”, translated here. https://www.henle.de/media/cb/cd/75/1697725893/1291-1697725893-sync.pdf

cues.title: Two hands sing together
cues.text: The march gives way to G major and a quieter two-beat measure, marked Poco tranquillo. A singing melody moves between the pianist’s hands. Soft chords surround the tune; the bustling bass of the opening has gone.
cues.evidence: Oesterle edition, bars 57–106: G major, 2/4, Poco tranquillo and cantando melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The publisher’s hotcakes
cues.text: On 21 December 1904, the publisher Henri Hinrichsen writes to Grieg that Wedding Day and the earlier Lyric Pieces are still much played and sell “like hotcakes”. The anniversary march has become a bestseller.
cues.evidence: Hinrichsen to Grieg, 21 December 1904, quoted in the Henle HN 1291 preface, p. III, from Benestad and Brock, Edvard Grieg: Briefwechsel mit dem Musikverlag C. F. Peters 1863–1907 (1997), p. 550. “Wie warme Semmeln” is translated here as “like hotcakes”. https://www.henle.de/media/cb/cd/75/1697725893/1291-1697725893-sync.pdf

cues.title: The march comes home
cues.text: D major returns with Tempo I. The low octaves, clipped chords and little triplet are back in their old places. After the quiet duet, the opening march sounds like a room filling with people again.
cues.evidence: Oesterle edition, bar 107 onwards: return to D major, 4/4 and Tempo I, followed by the opening material.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Grieg has the last word
cues.text: Little triplets keep dancing over low D octaves as the piano grows quieter: p, pp, then ppp, with the soft pedal down. Grieg saves one enormous D major chord for the end, marked fff. The party refuses to slip away unnoticed.
cues.evidence: Oesterle edition, bars 163 to the end: D pedal, triplets, unacorda, ppp and final fff chord with tre corde.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: The Bergen merchant’s son who put Norwegian fiddle tunes, a troll king and a wedding party into concert-hall music.
facts: Conductor in Christiania, 1866–74 · Harmonien, Bergen, 1880–82 · a state composer’s stipend from 1874
Rikard Nordraak 1864–65 · Piano Concerto 1869 · Peer Gynt 1876 · Troldhaugen 1885
Ten books of Lyric Pieces, about 170 songs, a piano concerto, stage music, a string quartet and five sonatas

quote.text: The most important thing is truth, the truth of feeling.
quote.source: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, May 1904, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon

composer.background:
Edvard Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in the family house at Strandgaten 152, above Bergen’s harbour. His father, Alexander, was a merchant and the British vice-consul; his mother, Gesine, who had studied singing, piano and theory in Hamburg, taught him the piano from the age of six. He hated scales. What he remembered, in his essay Min første Succes, was the day at five when he stretched up to the keyboard and found a third, a triad, a four-note chord and at last, with both hands, the five notes of a ninth. “That was a success!” he wrote. “Nothing since has been able to intoxicate me like this.”

In the summer of 1858 the violinist Ole Bull called without warning at the Griegs’ summer house at Landås. Edvard was made to play. Bull grew serious, talked quietly with the parents, then shook the boy in his own way and said: “You are going to Leipzig to become an artist!” On 6 October Grieg entered the Conservatory. He later called it “that damned Leipzig conservatory”, yet he went free to the Gewandhaus rehearsals, saw Tannhäuser fourteen times, and heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto. In the spring of 1860 tuberculosis ruined one of his lungs. That autumn, against the doctor’s advice, he went back.
